title: AI Watch: resolution calendar
intro: Dated moments when an open, AI-relevant question resolves, each paired with the specific observable that settles it. These are not predictions. Each row states what to watch and the tell that decides it.

rows.label: Late Jul 2026
rows.question: Is the AI data-centre capital-expenditure boom still accelerating?
rows.settles: Hyperscaler Q2 earnings: 2026 capex guidance raised, held or cut, plus memory (HBM) allocation commentary. A held-or-cut guide would be the first crack.
rows.matters: The buildout is the load-bearing assumption under current AI valuations.

anchor.label: Contingent vs Robust AI Power Demand

rows.label: 2 Aug 2026
rows.question: EU AI Act Article 50 transparency obligations take effect.
rows.settles: First enforcement posture and guidance on AI-content transparency and disclosure duties.
rows.matters: The first hard, dated EU AI Act obligation to bind AI products.

rows.label: 1 Oct 2026
rows.question: Are the Colorado River's 2007 operating rules replaced before they expire?
rows.settles: New interim operating guidelines agreed, or a deadlock. A deadlock raises litigation and water-siting risk for Western US data centres.
rows.matters: AI data-centre siting in the US Southwest turns on water and hydropower allocation.

rows.label: 27 Nov 2026
rows.question: Do China's rare-earth and neon export controls renew, widen or lapse?
rows.settles: The renewal decision, with neon controls the specific trigger to watch.
rows.matters: Neon and rare earths are chokepoints in the chip supply chain behind AI compute.

rows.label: 2 Dec 2027
rows.question: EU AI Act high-risk (Annex III) obligations take effect.
rows.settles: The high-risk compliance regime comes into force.
rows.matters: The heaviest tier of EU AI Act obligations, covering high-risk AI systems.

gauges.name: Strait of Hormuz risk
gauges.reading: Brent crossed $100 on 23 July and traded near $100 on 24 July, up roughly 14% on the week and from a low of $70.55 on 2 July. Triggered by reported tanker strikes off Saudi Arabia, Houthi attacks on two Saudi tankers in the Red Sea, and the Caspian Pipeline Consortium suspending Black Sea loadings.
gauges.watch: The $100 level flagged here on 13 July has now been crossed, so the tell moves on: whether it holds above $100 rather than whether it gets there. Goldman puts Brent above $120 in Q4 if Hormuz disruption persists.
gauges.context: This runs against the forecast anchor. The EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook base case of 7 July had Brent easing to about $70 by Q4 2026 as the tanker backlog cleared. Rapidan has since raised its Q4 estimate to near $100 from $85. The base case is not yet withdrawn by its author, but it is now the minority view and is recorded here as contested rather than quietly dropped.

deflations.claim: Memory prices "+355% by the end of this year"
deflations.corrected: Gartner: +125% across 2026; DRAM +100-116% Q1-26; TrendForce +13-18% QoQ Q3-26, cooling from ~60% QoQ in Q2; Counterpoint 80-90% QoQ Q4-25→Q1-26
deflations.error: No source exists for 355%. Probable mechanism: a supply-partner note advising customers to "plan for 10-20% per month" compounded across a year lands near a triple-digit figure ⇒ a planning ceiling read as a forecast. Note the direction of the real data is decelerating (Q2 ~60% QoQ → Q3 13-18%) while the claim implies acceleration. Added 2026-07-17 from the transcript sweep (IBM video)

deflations.claim: S&P top-10 concentration "~10% in 2000 vs 40% today"
deflations.corrected: ~23% in 2000 (Visual Capitalist; 20-25% across sources) vs ~36% today, off a ~41% peak in 2025
deflations.error: Both ends wrong in the direction that inflates the change: the claim implies a 4× rise, the data show 23→36, roughly 1.6×. The honest version of the point survives and is stronger for being smaller. ⭐ The caveat the same video omits, which cuts the other way: in 2000 tech was ~33% of S&P market cap on only ~15% of its earnings; today's top-10 weight sits on real profits, so weight alone is not equivalent excess. Added 2026-07-29 (transcript sweep)

deflations.claim: Margin debt "record $1.42T" as evidence of a top
deflations.corrected: level TRUE ($1.416T, May-2026, +8.5% m/m, +53.7% y/y), the INFERENCE fails on the denominator
deflations.error: ⭐ Same numerator, opposite story depending on the base. Against market cap margin debt is ~2.2%, BELOW the 2000 peak (~2.3%) and well below 2007 (~3.0%). Against GDP (~4%) it IS a record, just past Oct-2021's 3.97%. The video quotes only the nominal record, which is the one base that guarantees a record in any year prices rise. Also stale by two months when quoted. What genuinely survives: leverage grew at ~2× the pace of the S&P over the same May-to-May window, and only 1999-2000, mid-2007 and spring 2021 saw comparable growth RATES. Added 2026-07-29

deflations.claim: Banks tightening lending standards "~40% in 2023 → 8% today"
deflations.source: YouTube macro-strategy video [4], which books sales calls at the end
deflations.corrected: NOT CHECKABLE AS FRAMED, and the latest actual reading points the other way
deflations.error: The July-2026 SLOOS (Q2) is not published (the Fed releases it in early August), so no "today" figure exists. The most recent, April 2026, reports net TIGHTENING on C&I citing a less favourable outlook and reduced risk tolerance, plus tighter standards across all NDFI categories over the year. The video's entire "no recession, therefore buy the dip" thesis rests on this single series. ⚠️ SLOOS is reported as a net percentage (tightened minus eased), so a raw "8% of banks" reading would be a category error on top. Do not bank the 8%; re-check the series (FRED DRTSCILM) when the July release lands. Added 2026-07-29
